newsitem.title: UK: EMU to have positive impact on bond markets - S&P.
newsitem.headline: EMU to have positive impact on bond markets - S&P.

text.p: The changeover to a single currency in Europe is likely to have a profound and positive impact on bond market participants, Standard & Poor's Corp said.

European economic and monetary union (EMU) is unlikely to trigger substantial changes in most credit ratings, but it will eliminate the distinction between local and foreign currency debt for issuers within EMU, S&P analysts said.

EMU's fiscal discipline, low interest rates and reduced currency risk coupled with low operational costs, enhanced efficiency and liquidity would boost both the supply and demand sides of private debt markets, S&P said.
Once established, the European Central Bank will issue Euro- denominated debt for monetary policy purposes.

The debt is likely to be rated triple-A and will serve as a benchmark for other short-term debt instruments. Over time, obligations denominated in Euros of other triple-A borrowing institutions could act as benchmarks for Euro issues with longer-term maturities, S&P said.

"Meanwhile, Bunds issued by Germany, the largest and most creditworthy sovereign issuer expected to join EMU, should emerge as the de facto benchmark," European Ratings managing director George Dallas and European Ratings Development and Communications managing director Ian Mackintosh said.
The two analysts suggest three sectors are likely to evolve from EMU:
-- The new integrated Euro-denominated market, comprising existing local currency debt as well as private sector issues redenominated into Euros;

-- A continuing eurobond market comprised of issuance in various currencies which, given ongoing diversification of portfolios, could become even more global and may trend towards greater use of credit risk to gain relative performance; and
-- A Euro equivalent of the U.S. dollar Yankee market, made up of debt denominated in the new single currency, issued by non-European issuers and sold to institutional investors in the EMU region.

With these trends, issuers should be better positioned to tap into a bigger pool of funds, although the various regional governments, banks, insurance companies, and corporate issuers would individually account for a smaller proportion of total issuance in a broader marketplace.

"A number of local issuers that relied on name recognition in the past are now thinking of getting a credit rating to help them reach new investors and counterparties in the larger, post-EMU pool," Dallas and Mackintosh said.
The U.S., with its large single currency bond market, may offer useful clues to the effects of monetary union on an integrated new European bond market.
S&P said in the U.S., the corporate and to a lesser extent in the tax-exempt U.S. municipal bond markets relative values along the yield curve were dominated by credit factors.
In addition, an illiquidity premium could emerge for less liquid or smaller issues, it said.
